old: A little piece meaning 'again' has traveled from an ancient Italic root through Latin and French before landing quietly in English.
Attach 'again' to the front of a word meaning 'spot' or 'position,' and you'll find this verb.
Its cousin prefix re- shows up in words like return and reuse — here it's fused right onto 'place.'
clues: This everyday verb about what fills a spot wasn't borrowed whole from another language; English built it by joining a prefix meaning "again" or "back" to a common word.
It means taking away something worn out or broken and putting a new one in its spot, like a dead battery. Unlike repairing, the old item doesn't stay.
A beloved legend is someone nobody can ever do this to, and a library sign asks you to do it with books, setting each back on its shelf.
